decisions.why: This is a measured resource decision and touches no requested behavior.

The refusal of an undeclared reader is behavior, but its only reach is the soundness of the requested reuse: delete the reuse and it has nothing to check, so it enforces the request. Retiring FULL and INCREMENTAL=0 as reuse switches closes unrecorded escapes, which is enforcement of the request. The idle run keeping reuse extends reuse to a path the request does not mention rather than narrowing anything asked ('reuse ... results of tests which have already run ... is exactly what we should be doing'). decisions.why: The means of cutting the cost FR-012 asks cut; outputs held (coverage reports identical, 19 crates green, guard suite 37/37, 8 l7r-gate verbs identical).

decisions.why: A means of cutting link time and output size; the plan records coverage reports unchanged, so FR-012's hold on outputs is kept.

decisions.why: Choice among means for T96's cost; the deferred items are make static's coverage and dead-code reruns, which the GM filed as T100 and FR-012 assigns there, so nothing asked is dropped.

decisions.summary: After figures by the same make rust-test command (3.8 s to about 1 s for a claims edit) and make static after core and claims edits (103.3 to ~75 s, 64.8 to ~56 s), outputs re-verified.
decisions.why: SC-007's re-measure by the same command and verdict hold; every figure carries a one-shot observed/method label.

decisions.summary: A new guard, scratch-sweep-hooks, starts at most one detached sweep a day from UserPromptSubmit; make scratch-sweep [DRY=1] runs one on demand.
decisions.why: The GM: 'Fix those leaks as well' of the session scratch under /tmp/claude-1000; FR-013 asks for a sweep of finished sessions' scratch. A recurring sweep, with make as the one entry point (FR-005), is how the leak is fixed and nothing beyond it.

decisions.summary: A session directory goes when its transcript AND everything inside it have been unchanged three days; a session directory with no transcript and a loose top-level entry go when nothing inside changed in three days.
decisions.why: FR-013: swept 'once its transcript has been idle for days, never a live session's'. Also reading the directory's own contents is how 'never a live session's' is kept when a subagent writes there without touching the session's transcript, so it carries the spec's own constraint. Directories with no transcript and loose entries are scratch under /tmp/claude-1000 too, part of the 38 GB leak the GM said to fix, and are judged by the same idle rule.

decisions.summary: Three days idle, swept once a day, as GUESS knobs (SCRATCH_SWEEP_DAYS) with seams for the tests.
decisions.why: FR-013 says 'idle for days' and gives no number. Three days fills that in and also meets the relay's 'don't touch dirs younger than a few hours'.

decisions.summary: Always kept: the prompting session's directory, every session registered as running in ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json whose pid still runs and whose procStart matches, and any entry a live process holds as its cwd, binary or open file.
decisions.why: This is FR-013's 'never a live session's' itself. A session paused over a weekend has an idle transcript but is still live, so the registry and /proc checks are what make that clause hold.

decisions.summary: Where the session registry cannot be read, no session directory is judged at all.
decisions.why: Without the registry the sweep cannot tell a live session paused past three days from a finished one. Sweeping anyway would break FR-013's 'never a live session's', which is the GM's own constraint, so the exception is implied by the request's own words. It covers session directories only, and loose entries are still swept. Checked 2026-11-11 with ls -la ~/.claude/sessions/ on this container: the registry is present and readable by uid 1000, and its records carry pid and procStart. So the fail-safe is not the default on the machine that has the leak.

decisions.summary: Nothing is removed where /proc cannot be read.
decisions.why: Without /proc the sweep cannot see which entries live processes hold, so removing would risk exactly what FR-013 forbids. The exception is implied by 'never a live session's'. On this Linux container /proc is readable, so the case is a fail-safe and does not hollow out the sweep.

decisions.summary: Any tree containing a directory the sweep cannot read is kept.
decisions.why: The sweep cannot establish that nothing inside changed in three days, or that no live process holds it, without reading the tree. Removing it would need the idle test that FR-013 sets as the condition for sweeping, and that test cannot be run here, so the rule cannot be applied as written. The case is per-tree and does not exempt the readable scratch the leak is made of.

decisions.summary: Links are never followed or descended: a link inside a removed tree is deleted as itself with its target untouched, and a link at the root or among a project's sessions is left.
decisions.why: The scope is scratch UNDER /tmp/claude-1000, and following a link could delete or judge something outside it. A link at the root or in a session slot holds no disk itself, and its idleness and liveness could only be judged by following it out of the root, which the request's scope forbids. Leaving it frees nothing less, so the leak fix's purpose is untouched. Links inside a removed tree are still removed, so no scratch survives through them.

decisions.summary: The hook reads only the stamp's age and starts the sweep with setsid -f; the sweep takes a lock, rechecks the stamp and writes it before walking. Cost recorded with labeled figures.
decisions.why: This is how the sweep runs (cost and concurrency) and settles nothing about what is or is not swept. All figures carry observed-date and method labels.

decisions.summary: Every removal and the day's total are written to the guard log with sizes.
decisions.why: It makes the requested sweep checkable and adds no behavior.

decisions.summary: A dry run on this machine would remove 110 entries, 11.0 MB; the large trees were already cleared by the laptop session.
decisions.why: This is a labeled measurement. It does not conflict with FR-013's 'the existing pile is left to the GM's laptop session': the plan does not do a separate cleanup of the pile, the laptop session has already cleared the large trees, and the forward sweep that FR-013 asks for applies its idle rule to whatever is there.

decisions.summary: A project directory left empty is kept.
decisions.why: A project directory is a container for many sessions, not a finished session's scratch, which is the subject of FR-013 and SC-008. Empty, it holds no meaningful disk.

decisions.summary: Checklist part A: goal, constraints, order after T96 beside T101 (T102 extends to the cargo cache), exits through make land and arbiter-ask, and a done measure (504 tests passed, the dry run).
decisions.why: It restates FR-013 and records process, and narrows nothing. Its figures are labeled.

blocks: ### T102 (the cargo target cache stops growing, FR-013)

decisions.summary: The cargo target cache is pruned by extending T103's daily sweep (same lock, stamp, live-process check, log and make scratch-sweep [DRY=1]).
decisions.why: FR-013 and the GM's 'Fix those leaks as well' ask that the cache stop growing without bound and leave the mechanism open. A periodic prune is a direct means to that end and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: Within a store, each crate's variants beyond its newest four are removed once idle three days.
decisions.why: This bounds growth from moved paths and changed flags, which serves SC-008. One caveat: the premise that cargo makes a new variant only on a path or flag change is stated, not measured, and the bundle does not show how variants are grouped. Per-run-named crates (l7r_fixture_broken_<n>) would escape a per-name cap. What covers the measured leak is the dry run, which reports the l7r_fixture variants removed, and the fact that the source is gone. The cap's adequacy therefore rests on the dry run, not on the rule as written. That is a design caveat, not a narrowing: nothing the GM asked for is excluded.

decisions.summary: A build directory named for no live tree is removed whole after three idle days. The mirror's and every clone's directories are never removed whole. Where the clones directory cannot be read, nothing is removed whole.
decisions.why: Live trees' directories are still variant-pruned, so growth stays bounded. The protections keep the guard's binary and live builds safe, in line with the relayed caution not to touch what a running gate may own. Nothing asked for is narrowed.

decisions.summary: Anything a live process holds is kept, as in T103.
decisions.why: A safety condition in line with the relayed 'don't touch dirs ... a running gate may own'. It does not limit the leak fix.

decisions.summary: The sweep's first run removes stale content already in the cache: about 2.4 GB, including six stale build directories.
decisions.why: FR-013's 'the existing pile is left to the GM's laptop session' comes from the relayed message, where 'the existing pile' is defined in the preceding sentence as the /tmp l7r-* scratch directories (T101). The GM's only words on the cargo cache are 'Fix those leaks as well', and a sweep that fixes a growth leak necessarily removes what is stale. T103 did the same for /tmp/claude-1000 and was cleared. The three-day idle threshold and the live-process check go beyond the 'younger than a few hours' caution.

decisions.summary: Four variants and three idle days are new constants, labeled GUESS knobs.
decisions.why: These are parameters of the requested mechanism, declared as guesses and not claimed as measurements. They narrow nothing.

decisions.summary: 'Done, measured' is the dry run, with the mechanism pinned by fixture tests.
decisions.why: The dry run shows what the sweep removes today, not SC-008's property that the cache's size stops growing with test runs. The fixture tests cover the mechanism that gives that property. This is a plan-quality point and narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: l7r-gate rust test-counters runs a crate's counting build only where the crate has a `counters` feature and passes over the rest by name
decisions.why: FR-012 asks for the counters-inert phase's cost to be cut with every verdict held. The phase exists to prove the counters change no result, and a crate with no counters has nothing for it to prove. On the plan's labeled census (only rust/phases has the feature; core's testkit is already on under cfg(any(test, ...)); no other crate has features), the counting build of the other 18 crates was the default test build run a second time. That makes this removal of duplicate work, which is what was asked, not a narrowing of what is proven. The ruling rests on one premise the plan states without a method label: that make static's cover runs those same default tests in the same make done. The implementation has to keep that true.

decisions.summary: the phase's output changes: a pass-over line per skipped crate replaces its test run
decisions.why: FR-012's 'every output and verdict' clause is there so that results do not move. A pass-over line reports work not repeated and is not a changed result. Every verdict still comes out the same: from cover for the skipped crates, and from the unchanged counting run for rust/phases.

decisions.summary: rustc crate tests give a crate a `counters` feature where they run the counting build and assert the pass-over line for one without
decisions.why: Enforcement of the requested change: if the gating were deleted, the test would have nothing left to check. It is not unrequested scope.

decisions.summary: measurement: before from two landings' make done counters-inert phase (113 s, 59 s); after from make counters-inert FRESH=1 (4.96 s) plus T97's own landing's counters-inert phase
decisions.why: FR-012 and SC-007 require the before and after figures to come from the same command. Item 9 (Done, measured), with a one-landing budget, makes the counters-inert phase of the landing that carries T97 a done condition, and that is the same command as the before figure. SC-007 is satisfied by that landing-phase figure, which must be recorded. The FRESH=1 timing does not satisfy it, because it is a different command and is only supplementary evidence. If the landing-phase figure were deferred past T97's landing, this would become a narrowing, and an illegitimate one.

decisions.summary: the gate is keyed on a feature literally named `counters`
decisions.why: The phase is the counters-inert phase, and today's labeled census finds the counters under exactly that feature name in the one crate that has them. No case that exists today is excluded.

decisions.summary: ordered after T101-T103; one landing; red exit via make arbiter-ask; no engine code or map change
decisions.why: Sequencing and procedure inside FR-012. None of it narrows the request or the spec.

blocks: ### T111 (a coverage pass records the crate's test result, FR-012)

decisions.summary: A passing `l7r-gate rust cover` run on a crate whose `cargo test` is its unit tests alone keeps that crate's `test` key green, so `make rust-test` after `make static` does not rerun those tests.
decisions.why: This is the GM's own words of 2026-11-11 ('a passing coverage run recording the test result', approved with 'Yes to all 4 of those, please'), carried into FR-012 as T111.

decisions.summary: The coverage run's tests count as the plain tests because the coverage build differs only by instrumentation and cfg(coverage), and no Rust source reads cfg(coverage).
decisions.why: This argues that the recorded result is the same verdict the plain run would give, which FR-012 requires ('held to every output and verdict the tooling gives today'). The premise was observed and dated with its method rather than assumed, and it narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: A crate whose `cargo test` covers more than its lib unit tests (binaries, src/bin, tests/, examples, benches, a [[bin]]-style manifest table, doctests) keeps no test result from a coverage pass. This currently leaves out rust/guard, rust/gate, rust/phases and rust/gate/crates/rustc.
decisions.why: Taken literally, the request would record a result for the whole crate on every passing coverage run. For these crates that cannot be true: the coverage run (`cargo test --no-run --lib`) never builds or runs their binary, integration, example, bench or doc tests, so a passing coverage run has no result for them to record. Recording one anyway would mark tests green that never ran, which breaks FR-012's requirement that every verdict the tooling gives today is held, and that requirement comes from the GM's own words. The carve-out is limited to the tests the coverage run does not execute, and each excluded class is the same kind of thing (a test the coverage run did not run), so one argument covers them all. One separate point affects whether the exclusion is wide enough, not whether it is legitimate. The detection is described as finding doctests by a doc comment with a code FENCE. Rustdoc also compiles and runs indented code blocks in doc comments as doctests, and the 2026-11-11 observation searched for fences only. A crate with an indented doctest would therefore have its doctests skipped. The detection should treat any doc code block as a doctest, or check that none exists.

blocks: ### T111 (a coverage pass records the crate's test result, FR-012)

The equivalence premise (no code reads cfg(coverage)) is measured, with a one-shot label, not assumed.

decisions.summary: A crate whose cargo test also runs binaries, integration tests, examples, benches or doctests (today rust/guard, rust/gate, rust/phases, rust/gate/crates/rustc) keeps no test result from a coverage pass.
decisions.why: In those crates the coverage run does not run all the tests cargo test runs, so keeping the crate's whole test key green would record a result for tests that never ran. That breaks FR-012/SC-007's 'held to every output and verdict', and it is outside the GM's own purpose: reuse the results of tests 'which have already run'. On a crate-level key, the literal rule cannot be honored without a false verdict. Each class was checked separately: binaries, integration tests, examples, benches and doctests are all cases the coverage run does not execute, so one argument covers all of them. Which crates fall out is decided by inspecting each crate (unit_tests_only), not by a fixed list. The measured result (18 of 19 crates standing after a core edit, against 11 before) shows the purpose is served, not gutted. The lib tests of the excluded crates still run twice. Recording them separately would be a further saving, not something the request requires.

decisions.summary: Only the test key make rust-test asks first is kept. The second key, over the plain test binaries, is not, because asking it would build them.

It is legitimate because applying it literally would defeat the request's own stated constraint (FR-012/SC-007: every output and verdict held): rustfmt formats comments and the dead check counts a word in a comment as a use, so a key blind to comments would reuse a verdict a comment can change. blocks: ### T115 (the full hook run's two longest suites, FR-012)

decisions.summary: The record's pages are parsed across the cores before Record::of reads them (warm in record/units.rs); the parse table's lock is taken only to look up and to keep; the record is then read in the same order from the same parses.
decisions.why: A means to the GM's 'the full hook run's two longest suites' (FR-012, T115). FR-012's 'held to every output and verdict' is carried by the block's own evidence: record-owed with no flags, --unanswered and --slugs, on an empty delta and with a page edited, byte-identical between the old and new binaries (cmp). Nothing narrowed.

decisions.summary: push-checks' rows start at once; each row's output is shown in the table's order; the first refusal ends the run with the shell's line as before.
decisions.why: Table order, verdict and the refusal's shell line are held as FR-012 requires, and the test the_runner_stops_at_the_first_refusal_with_the_shell_s_line pins the verdict. The one output that moves is split out as T115-D3 and ruled there.

decisions.summary: Within one row, the row's stdout is shown before its stderr, so where a row wrote to both the cross-stream interleave can differ from today's.
decisions.why: Narrows FR-012's 'held to every output'. Legitimate on the impossibility bar, scoped tightly: when rows run at once their output has to be captured, and two captured pipes carry no shared order; a single merged capture (pipe or pty) keeps the order but moves stderr bytes onto stdout, which is itself an output change. So every concurrent design changes one of the two, and only a serial run changes neither. A serial run would give sync-with-main, one of the two suites the GM named for T115, nothing from this task, since push-checks is the block's only lever on that suite; so the literal rule would defeat half the request. The ruling covers ONLY the stdout/stderr interleave within a single row, replayed after that row ends. Each stream's bytes and their order within the stream, the table order, the refusal line and the verdict are not excepted and must stay as they are today. Any wider output difference is not approved here.

decisions.summary: Rows after a refusal now run (today they do not), but show nothing and keep nothing; a self-test after a refusal is not kept.
decisions.why: If 'keeps nothing' holds, no output or verdict moves; running wasted work is cost, not fidelity. A seam the block should close in its text: it says the two memo presets and the ledger check each keep a file of their own by atomic rename, and its parenthetical says only how a self-test after a refusal is withheld. Nothing says how a memo or ledger row that has already run is stopped from renaming its file into place. The block should name that mechanism, or say that such a file is kept. Not blocking: a kept memo records a true pass for that tree state, so a later verdict is unchanged.

decisions.summary: The full hook run's wall time is left as it is (measured unchanged, 64.8/64.4 s before vs 64.6/64.2 s after, bound by contention the suites share in the kernel); it is offered to the GM as a candidate, not changed here.
decisions.why: The GM's words for T115 name 'the full hook run's two longest suites', not the full run's wall time. The block measures the suites lower inside the full run (sync-with-main 51.9/52.9 to 49.1/48.5 s, entry-gate 47.8/47.0 to 43.0/44.3 s), reports openly that the full run did not move, and leaves the kernel-bound cause to the GM instead of quietly widening scope. That is the right way to handle it.

decisions.why: No constant moved; 12 and 16 were measured slower (72.8 s, 76.3 s vs 64.1 s), so the existing value is kept. Nothing narrowed.

decisions.summary: Normalizations N3 (the line 'This report took X s') and N5 (the hook's own time in a written line).
decisions.why: Byte equality on a wall-clock time is physically impossible: two runs of the Python itself do not match there. Only the time value is normalized; the line's presence and every other byte stay compared, so FR-002's purpose (the port gives the same answers) is intact.

decisions.summary: Normalization N4: the order of where-time rows that tie on their sort key; the Python left it to its string hash (two PYTHONHASHSEED values gave two orders), the Rust keeps the order first booked.
decisions.why: There is no single Python output to hold the Rust to: the Python's order was observed to move with the hash seed, so matching it byte for byte is physically impossible. The rows themselves stay compared; only the order among rows equal on the sort key is normalized, which carries no information the report's reader relies on. A deterministic order is the only way to have one output at all.

decisions.summary: Normalization N6: the Makefile's path in make's own error line.
decisions.why: An artifact of the harness comparing HEAD's Makefile at one path with this clone's at another; it is make's text, not an output of the ported tool.

decisions.summary: Disclosed divergences no case reaches: non-ASCII digits in an int or float, NaN in JSON, unhashable or mixed-type event fields, a list-valued t on a lone event, which agent wins when one tool id is in two subagents' transcripts, non-UTF-8 git output (both fail, at different points), and -h exiting 2.

(c) Non-UTF-8 git output: both fail, so the verdict is held. (d) Non-ASCII digits, NaN, unhashable or mixed-type fields, a list-valued t: inputs no held case and none of the real features, logs and transcripts in the 182-case differential produced; FR-002 binds 'every case its tests and its suites hold', and the list is disclosed rather than excluded from a held case. blocks: ### T142 (ticked tasks archived out of tasks.md, the GM 2026-11-15)

decisions.summary: Every ticked task with an id (lowercase `- [x] Tnn`) and its indented lines moves to tasks-done.md, unless it holds an open box; the GM-review box, headings, Occasions and prose stay; no recent ticked tasks kept; blocks byte for byte in id order; one pointer line, no per-block marker.
decisions.why: The GM asked for tooling that moves completed tasks out of tasks.md so it stops eating tokens. A ticked task that still holds an open box is not completed work (it holds a landing), and the GM box is an open review state, not a finished task, so keeping them is not a carve-out from the request. The tick itself treats only lowercase [x] as ticked and writes it that way, so every task finished through the tooling moves. Moving all finished tasks instead of keeping a few recent ones reads 'old completed tasks' at its widest and serves the token purpose.

decisions.summary: Every tick archives all of its feature's ticked tasks, plan section or not; make plan-archive and `tick --archive` move them by hand; 449 archived in the cut; closed features are not backfilled; the tick-archive usage line is recorded on every tick.
decisions.why: 'Automatically move' is carried by the tick. The purpose is long-running features worked on now, and each open feature clears at its next tick. The request asks for the mechanism, not a migration of closed features, so not backfilling does not take any case away from it, and the manual command stays available for any feature. The tool-yield shift is a side effect, not new behavior.

decisions.summary: One reader/mover in the guard's shared::speckit::tasks; the readers that need ticked tasks (state, approval at_rev, plan checks, next id, already-ticked, spec lint, report) read both files; readers of open tasks only keep reading tasks.md, from a stated grep census.
decisions.why: Without this, the archive would break readers: a feature would read as reopened, an archived id could be handed out again, and so on. Wiring the readers to the moved file is what makes the requested move correct (FR-003, one implementation). The enumeration states its search space.

decisions.summary: The tick's block end becomes any heading (it was only `## `, so a `###` heading got swallowed and 449's T001/T005/T070 were misplaced, repaired before the archive; closed 383/417 left as history); a refused land batch removes the tasks-done.md/plan-done.md its tick created.
decisions.why: The archive moves blocks by the tick's own block boundary, so a boundary that swallows a heading would carry that heading into tasks-done.md. A refused landing that leaves the new archive file untracked would leave the tree half-moved. Both fixes exist only so that the requested move is correct. Leaving closed features' history alone is not a narrowing of anything the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: A before/after comparison over every feature archived in a copy (1,001 outputs, none differing); the archived lookup reads lowercase [x] alone to match the tick's rule; an end-to-end make run; 449's sizes; static, rust-test and hooks-test green.
decisions.why: These are checks that only fail if the requested archive changes what any reader answers, or if it does not happen. That is enforcement of the request and FR-002, not a property the GM never mentioned. The lowercase rule keeps the archived lookup consistent with the tick, so it is not a carve-out.

decisions.summary: Done before the phase-4 slices, which file their tasks into the archived tasks.md; budget one landing.
decisions.why: This is sequencing within the feature. It takes nothing out of the request.

blocks: ### T146 (phase 4's S3a, the one browser crate, `ask:449-phase4-slices`)

decisions.summary: archive.py's logic ported to a new gate crate `archive`; its browser a new crate rust/browser/ (l7r-browser serve and crop) outside the gate's and guard's builds, no gate or guard crate depending on it
decisions.why: FR-001 / ask:449-T80-order (4) as amended by ask:449-T146-browser: a client of its own in its own binary, out of the guards' and gate's build path; ask:449-phase4-slices S3a.

decisions.summary: The browser client speaks the DevTools protocol over --remote-debugging-pipe itself, launched with Playwright's switches and page setup, instead of chromiumoxide or headless_chrome
decisions.why: Exactly what the round arbiter ruled in ask:449-T146-browser (2026-11-16), written into FR-001 and T80-order (4): a DevTools-pipe client of its own, lighter than both named crates (9 against 92 and 118, one-shot labeled).

decisions.summary: scripts/record/glyph_crop.py ported to `l7r-browser crop` and deleted in this cut; depiction.rs runs it through l7r-gate.sh browser crop
decisions.why: ask:449-phase4-slices: S3a is archive.py and glyph_crop on the one browser crate; ask:449-T88-bundles moves modal_bundle.glyph_crop onto the CDP crate. 36 crop pairs compared, none differing.

decisions.summary: archive.py cut to the reads its importers use plus forwarders for every write and the browser, until S3b and S4 delete it
decisions.why: FR-001 places uncited/uncited_imports/archive_ops in S3b and research_search/semantic_index in S4; half-ported reads with one writer is the ask:449-T81-slices / ask:449-T86-door pattern under FR-003.

decisions.summary: This slice wires the Rust into production callers (Makefile archive recipes, record::reserve in process, depiction.rs's crop, tree's stamp, Python writes forwarded) rather than landing a library with no production caller
decisions.why: ask:449-phase4-slices' default slice shape (library, Python staying the implementation) yields here to the more specific ask:449-T80-order (4), which phase4-slices itself invokes for S3a's order and which moves the Chromium install off the Python package in the same cut, with T145's precedent under ask:449-T88-bundles. It ports more, not less, of what the GM asked ('all be ported to Rust'), and the purpose of the slice shape, one wired implementation (FR-003, FR-001c), holds: each file has one live writer, the Rust, with the 13 importer cases in the differential. Nothing the request or spec asked for is narrowed.

decisions.summary: chromium.pin pins Chrome for Testing headless shell 151.0.7922.34 by SHA-256 (the build Playwright 1.62 installed); install-chromium.sh replaces `playwright install` in setup-dev-env.sh; the Playwright package stays in requirements-dev.in until S7 ports page_lit, page_lit launching the pinned Chromium via executable_path; tree's stamp salts the browser area with the pinned version
decisions.why: ask:449-T80-order (4): 'the Chromium install moved off the Python package in setup-dev-env.sh in the same cut' - the install moves, the package is not required to go; page_lit is S7's (ask:449-phase3-remainder, phase4-slices) and FR-001 places setup-dev-env.sh's Python and requirements in phase 4. The salt keeps cache keys correct.

decisions.summary: The plain GET runs curl, sharing the page context's cookies as Playwright's request context did
decisions.why: Implementation of the port, T145's fetch precedent; the 109-case differential (cookies, redirects, PDFs, binary, 404s) holds the outputs (FR-002).

decisions.summary: Node's words kept for the failures the Python's reports name (refused, not found, timeout, redirect cap); other fetch failures carry curl's own error text
decisions.why: An FR-002 output not held byte for byte, so narrowing. ask:449-T066-json-message is a general ruled case - where a message quotes a library's own error text inside a fixed message, verdict, exit, location and fixed words match and the quoted text is the replacement's - with the spec lint as its instance, not its limit. The plan holds more than the ruling requires (the named failures keep Node's words) and lets only the quoted library text of unnamed failures change. curl is a program rather than a Rust library, but the ruling's purpose - a port cannot reproduce another fetch library's own error strings - applies unchanged. No case in the 109 surfaced such a difference.

decisions.summary: The archive's working copy and manifest rows written by the Rust alone; archive.py's ensure, push, place_gm, archive_url, _lane, settle, sync_gm_copies, write_row, Browser, fetch and wayback forward to door verbs; reads, the lock and Archive's git reads stay Python; a Rust verb run by a Python caller under that lock takes no lock itself
decisions.why: FR-003 and ask:449-T86-door (one implementation writing each file, door verbs, no logic in the door); ask:449-T81-slices allows the reads to stay half-ported. Not re-taking the caller's lock prevents self-deadlock without opening a second writer.

decisions.summary: One seam (Reach, cli_with) replaces store, browser and credential in the crates' tests; one kept end-to-end case in tests/hooks/test-l7r-gate.sh drives record archive url, backfill and gm-copies through the real launcher on the pinned Chromium, a local bare remote, empty secrets and a dead proxy
decisions.why: ask:449-T80-order (4): 'behind one seam, one end-to-end test'; FR-008 exempts the one end-to-end test from the tenth-of-a-second bar; ask:449-T146-browser's 'its one end-to-end test'.

decisions.summary: The production wiring that hands in the real store, browser and credential (cli, production_store, start_browser, token, Process::start) is #[cfg(not(test))], so it is outside the unit-test coverage instrument and reached only by the end-to-end case
decisions.why: FR-004 read strictly asks every line reached by a test; these lines leave the instrument's denominator, so narrowing. Legitimate because the literal alternative is impossible within the spec: an instrumented unit test reaching start_browser or Process::start would start the real Chromium and network, which FR-008's tenth-of-a-second bar forbids, while the spec's own words (T80-order (4) and ask:449-T146-browser: one seam, one end-to-end test, FR-004 'with its one end-to-end test') put these lines on that test. The ruling depends on the excluded set being only the named hand-in of real store, browser, credential and process, as the block lists; any logic behind cfg(not(test)) beyond that is not covered by this ruling. Evidence gap noted: the block's label for 'executes every line of those blocks' (run, and run with no Chromium) shows the case depends on Chromium, not line reach.

decisions.summary: make archive-find, dead on AttributeError since T145 cut attempts.report, restored by a forwarder
decisions.why: Restores behavior FR-002 bound T145 to keep; the forwarder reaches the Rust, so FR-003's one implementation holds.

decisions.summary: The Rust archive-sources deadlock (stdout lock held while lanes printed) fixed
decisions.why: A defect in the port itself, fixed so its outputs match the Python's (FR-002).

decisions.summary: S1's entry_bodies read the whole registry per entry; fixed, cited from 8.7 s to 74 ms with the same output
decisions.why: A fix in already-ported Rust that this cut calls, holding the output; it serves the request's stated purpose (the code's inefficiency) and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: fancy_regex back-references matched case-sensitively where Python ignored case; the pattern spells the cases out
decisions.why: A port defect fixed toward the Python's behavior (FR-002).

decisions.summary: Chromium given its own directory instead of leaving files in TMPDIR
decisions.why: FR-013: the tooling must not leave what it makes on disk.

decisions.summary: HEAD's Python and Playwright against the Rust in network namespaces with recorded pages and a local bare remote, every output and file compared over 109 cases; normalizations limited to values two Python runs differ in (stamps, times, MHTML boundary, Content-IDs, Date, soft breaks, sorted server log, git log as multiset) plus traceback text and argparse text on exit 2
decisions.why: FR-002's comparison; normalizing run-to-run nondeterminism of the Python itself loosens nothing it binds, and traceback and argparse text are excluded by the ruled case ask:449-usage-text. T80-order (4)'s measurement on real sources stands as the replay of recorded real archive pages.

decisions.summary: The one differing case, archive_ops find, is held to the pre-T145 Python (b5a370293^) instead of HEAD's, which crashes on T145's defect
decisions.why: A departure from FR-002's literal baseline (HEAD's Python) with no ask behind it, so narrowing. Literal matching would require the Rust to reproduce an AttributeError crash that T145's own port introduced in breach of FR-002, defeating FR-002's purpose (the tools keep doing what they did) and the request's (a working Rust tool). FR-002's own exception, a check that refuses correct work today fixed in its port with the change named, covers it, and the block names it and shows the pre-T145 Python and the Rust agreeing on exit, stdout, stderr and attempts written across all four forms.

decisions.summary: The FR-002 case ask:449-T146-browser ruled on for uncited fetch with a blocked page is not taken, its premise (a Playwright crash at HEAD) shown to be a harness error; the lane's output with the blocked page mid-way held by a kept case
decisions.why: Declining a ruled exception and holding the full FR-002 output is the strict reading, not a narrowing.

decisions.summary: Timings (archive pages, a 96 MB page, crops, the installer) recorded and not held
decisions.why: No requirement binds this task to a timing; FR-010 measures at phase ends.

decisions.summary: No measurements.json names archive.py, glyph_crop or playwright; exits make static, rust-test, hooks-test HOOKS_ALL=1 and a gated land; ordered after S2 (T145)
decisions.why: FR-001's rewrite of recorded measurements in the porting commit; ask:449-phase4-slices' slice order; FR-004 coverage held by make static.

blocks: ### T161 (the GM's second approved proposal, the differentials rerunning only what a fix touched, enforced by tooling; request.md 2026-11-16, the GM 2026-11-11)

decisions.summary: One shared differential runner, l7r-gate diff-run in a new Rust gate crate, used by every port task's comparison from T147 on in place of hand-written driver loops
decisions.why: It is the GM's approved second proposal of 2026-11-16 ('the differentials rerunning only what a fix touched' ... 'please proceed with that'); Rust is FR-001's rule for new tooling, and it carries FR-002's comparison rather than changing it.

decisions.summary: Case shape: per-side world built by a setup command into a fresh directory, both sides as command templates, per-case steps, outputs compared (exit, stdout, stderr, every file written under the world, named extra files), one results row a case
decisions.why: Takes the shape the T143-T146 harnesses share, so no case is lost moving onto it; the outputs compared are at least what FR-002 binds (verdicts and outputs).

decisions.summary: Named normalizations (regex and replacement), each listed in the report as taken
decisions.why: The runner provides and reports the facility; it pre-authorizes no particular normalization, so FR-002's binding of outputs is not relaxed by this block - each normalization a port uses still answers to FR-002 and its ruled cases, and is visible in the report.

decisions.summary: The old side's result is kept on a key over the case definition, its normalizations, declared inputs and the old side's fingerprint (its files, the Python tree at its revision), so a port fix never reruns it
decisions.why: The old Python does not change under a port fix (FR-003 keeps it as is until replaced); any change to what it runs from moves its key. Rerunning it would only repeat a result the key proves unchanged - exactly the 'rerunning only what a fix touched' the GM approved.

decisions.summary: The new side's key uses the content of the source paths a case declares it exercises instead of the whole binary (whole new-side fingerprint when none declared), so an incremental run can keep a new-side result on a hand-written declaration
decisions.why: On the incremental path a kept new-side result rests on a declaration that can be too narrow, which is less than FR-002's 'every case'. Legitimate because it is the GM's own words ('rerunning only what a fix touched', 2026-11-16) and because the block itself preserves FR-002's purpose: the figures a plan reports come from --verify, one run of every case's new side against the kept old sides, named in the report as a verify run. The ruling rests on that sentence; the lint as described checks only that a diff-run report is cited, not that it is a verify run, so verify-backing is a stated rule rather than a tool-enforced one (noted, not blocking: the block does not relax FR-002).

decisions.summary: --verify reruns every case's new side at the end and is the source of a plan's reported figures; --only <name> reruns one case
decisions.why: --verify is what keeps FR-002's every-case proof under incremental reruns; --only is a narrower rerun, the direction the GM's 2026-11-11 words ask for.

decisions.summary: --twice runs the old side twice and reports what differs, as evidence a normalization covers only run-to-run noise
decisions.why: Moves into the runner a check T146's harness already did by hand; it bounds normalizations, serving FR-002, and adds no behavior the request lacks.

decisions.summary: Incremental rerun is the runner's default
decisions.why: The GM 2026-11-11: 'our tooling must enforce this' so sessions do not drift back to the slowest command; the default is that enforcement.

decisions.summary: --all (every side of every case) takes REASON= of two words or more, recorded in the report and the guard log, as FR-011's escapes do
decisions.why: Same escape shape FR-011 already gives make rust-test and make static; it enforces the requested incremental default and does not forbid the full run.

decisions.summary: make decide's lint refuses a sentence stating a differential's case count (cases beside 'differential' or FR-002's 'same outputs') that cites no diff-run runner report
decisions.why: Enforcement of the requested thing - port differentials going through the runner that reruns only what a fix touched - as the GM's 2026-11-11 rule asks ('our tooling must enforce this'). Note: it is a refusing guard and the block does not bound which features or tasks make decide applies it to; the GM's enforcement rule is not feature-limited, so not ruled out of scope, but its reach is worth stating in the plan.

decisions.summary: What a world needs beyond a setup command (network namespace, loopback server, bare remote) stays the harness's setup script, which the runner runs and keys
decisions.why: No class of case escapes the runner: the setup script is still run by it and is part of the key, so such cases still rerun only when touched. Only native modelling of those worlds is left out, which the request never asked for.

decisions.summary: Order after T159 and before T147 (its first user); exits: the crate's tests and coverage including named rerun/keep/verify/--all/lint cases, make land green; done measured by T147's runner reports counting reruns and kept sides, figures from a verify run
decisions.why: Order follows the GM's ranked list (figure check first, then the differentials); FR-004 coverage held; the exit tests check the requested behavior.

decisions.summary: Classed 'Performance work? No' - it saves an agent's waiting on reruns, not the tools' running time
decisions.why: The task is filed under the GM's direct approval of 2026-11-16, not the 2026-11-12 conditional pre-approval, so that pre-approval's measured-target condition does not govern it; it still carries a dated, methoded measurement of the wait it targets. The classification narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: uncited.py, uncited_imports.py and archive_ops.py ported (new gate crate `uncited`, archive operations into the `archive` crate) and deleted; attempts.py and reserve-prefix.py, imported by no Python any more, deleted
decisions.why: FR-001 and ask:449-phase4-slices S3b / ask:449-T80-order (3) place exactly this cluster; deleting a ported file is the GM's standing approval (FR-001, 2026-11-10).

decisions.summary: make uncited, cite-uncited, archive-sources, archive-inbox, archive-find, downloads ingest, record sources outcome cited: and uncited install wired to the Rust in this cut, Python by-path runs retired
decisions.why: Departs from the letter of ask:449-phase4-slices ('a slice lands its Rust as a library with no production caller'), but toward the request (the GM 2026-11-15: port until all tooling is ported) and not against that rule's purpose: the callers are make targets and Rust crates, no Python importer of these files remains, and Python stays the implementation for S4's importers. It does more of what was asked, so it narrows nothing; it does make the task non-straight under FR-001c, which this review covers.

decisions.summary: archive.py and sources.py cut to the names S4's research_search.py and semantic_index.py import (read-only names plus the `push` door); door verbs only the deleted importers used retire
decisions.why: The ask:449-T81-slices test and ask:449-phase4-slices (Python stays for Python importers until wired); doors are deleted with their last caller on the spec's T065 pattern.

decisions.summary: The filter's three lists written by uncited::lists alone; every other write through the one writer S2/S3a gave it
decisions.why: FR-003 as written.

decisions.summary: relayout (no caller) and verify --sample (CPython's Mersenne Twister and random.sample ported so a seed draws the same sample) ported, not dropped
decisions.why: Porting rather than dropping keeps FR-002's same outputs; dropping would have been the narrowing.

decisions.summary: rglob's CPython 3.14 listing order reproduced in archive::ops; research::pyre folds U+0130/U+0131 with i/I under an inline i flag as CPython re.I does, moving only (?i) patterns; archive_urls uses one browser for all its URLs, outputs the same
decisions.why: Each moves the Rust toward the Python's outputs (FR-002); the browser change is an implementation choice with outputs held equal (FR-006's one-process direction). Unmeasured premise noted, not blocking: 'the five in uncited; prepass's one other translates as before' carries no method, and it can only widen what matches CPython.

decisions.summary: T146's kept blocked-page case becomes uncited::fetch's unit test (same words, 120-char cut); tests/hooks/test-l7r-gate.sh runs the Rust production paths on the real browser behind dead proxies
decisions.why: The Python lane it drove is deleted; the case moves to the Rust whole, and the end-to-end test stays the one FR-008 and ask:449-T146-browser allow.

decisions.summary: Differential normalizations taken under ruled cases: the JSON parser's words in install's refusal, argparse's usage/error text (also before make's line), uncaught traceback text

The one possible downside, a too-narrow path list reading as agreement, is closed by construction: the report a plan may cite is always a whole-checkout verify, with no sparse result standing in it, and a test fails with that rule removed. Nothing the GM asked is narrowed; FR-002/FR-001c's comparison is still made on whole worlds. Figures carry observed-date and method labels.

It enforces the claims tracking the GM asked to have on Rust units (2026-11-17, T165) and the pilot's no-brainer fixes; no requested behavior is narrowed and no judgment-call downside is introduced.

decisions.summary: The shared differential runner keeps each worker's world for the run, one per side, and resets it to the side's revision between cases (outside emptied, .git restored from the copy taken at its making, read-tree -u --reset HEAD, clean -ffdx, WORKTREE laid over again, modes restored, setup rerun).
decisions.why: The GM, 2026-11-18: 'those efficiency improvements are worth making next. Please make those, then proceed with continuing the porting', on the standing 2026-11-12 condition of a concrete target with a measured saving (the tests' and landing's time first). Target measured before: the checkout 1.25-1.33 s and removal 0.27-0.30 s of each side, against a 0.1-0.2 s reset. After: 152.4 s to 51.0 s and 376.1 s to 164.5 s. FR-002's bar is kept on the instrument: all 640 kept results byte for byte the fresh worlds' except their time field, and every report row agrees with the earlier verify.

decisions.summary: A fresh world is made instead when the repository's HEAD or refs moved, the checkout's declaration or a GIT_ variable changed, or a reset step fails.
decisions.why: This guards the reuse's correctness, so a reused world never stands in for a revision it does not hold. It narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: Reuse is the default. --fresh-worlds keeps the old way.
decisions.why: A speed-up to the verify runs, which is what the 2026-11-18 request asks for. The old behavior stays reachable. The default rests on equality tests in which dropping any reset step, swapping read-tree for reset --hard, keeping a case's index, ignoring moved refs or losing the index time turns a test red.

decisions.summary: A reset world's file times are not compared with a fresh world's and do differ: untouched files keep the first checkout's time.
decisions.why: A fresh world never fixed file times either, since each checkout stamps its own arbitrary time, so no kept case's verdict can rest on their absolute values. The measured run shows no kept case depends on the relative times the reuse changes: 640 results are byte for byte the fresh worlds'. This is a limit of the speed-up's equality, stated openly. It does not narrow FR-002's requirement that a port's outputs match the Python's. --fresh-worlds remains for any case later found to read file times.

decisions.summary: Sparse worlds stay fresh and are not reused.
decisions.why: The optimisation is simply not applied to one world kind, which keeps that kind's existing behavior. The request names no world kind to be reused, and the measured goal (a third to a half of a port's verify time) is met without them. Nothing the GM asked for is carved out.

decisions.why: This is the request itself (2026-11-18): 'amend our project guidelines and speckit constitution and whatever else we need to update to clarify this and remove any references to things needing to be bitwise identical'. The arbiter's agent file is included, and the arbiter's ruling is what prompted the request.

decisions.summary: FR-002's ruled cases that excused only a byte difference are folded into the rule. The three that set a verdict or a behavior (T038 garbage stdin, T75 gatecost class, T72 coverage-exempt) are kept.
decisions.why: The collapsed cases each held a port to bytes until a ruling excused them, which is the 'ask/ruling for an exactness' the GM objected to. The kept three rule on what a tool DOES, not on its bytes, so the request does not reach them.

decisions.summary: Kept as not being a port's exactness standard: reproducibility (same code and seed give the same map; the cache audit; counters that must not change a map), a lossless split's integrity, a file hash naming its content, and a quotation verbatim from its source.
decisions.why: The GM's words carry the qualifier 'as an exactness standard', and his complaint is that 'things must match' what a port replaces. Each item here compares code with itself, or content with its own hash, or a quote with its source. None is agreement between a port and the thing it replaces.

decisions.summary: Past specs, dated records and history are left as written, and so are finished tasks' plan sections as records of what they measured.
decisions.why: This narrows 'remove any references' literally, but the GM's words name what is to change: 'our project guidelines and speckit constitution and whatever else we need to update to clarify this'. That is the guidance a session follows. A finished feature's spec and a dated record are not guidance for a port going forward, so leaving them does not leave a byte standard in force. Rewriting them would also falsify dated records, including the GM's own verbatim words in gm-rulings.md. The purpose (no future port held to bytes) is not touched. Condition: 'past specs' means features that are finished. A live spec still governing work is guidance and falls under T180-sweep.

decisions.summary: The one measure kept exact is the audit checks' verdicts (each check on each sheet, each guard's verdict on each suite case), and a check that refuses correct work is still fixed in its port.
decisions.why: This is the GM's own condition, 'so long as everything works' (2026-11-18), with 'so long as the changes don't violate our research findings' (2026-10-18, the standing rule FR-002 quotes). The checks' verdicts are how this project decides that everything works and that the research claims hold. Keeping them is the GM's condition, not a byte standard.

decisions.summary: rust/mode_a's lockstep tests stay until a harmless difference makes one fail. At that point the test is changed to hold the verdicts and claims (engine-plan.md condition 3 restated: 'a test may show agreement, bytes are not required').
decisions.why: This is live enforcement, not a record, so it cannot rest on T180-records-as-written. It passes the purpose test on its own terms. The GM's purpose is that a port is never stopped, narrowed or sent for a ruling because its bytes differ. A lockstep test that passes stops nothing. The one moment it could act as a byte standard is when a harmless difference fails it, and the decision then requires the test to be changed, not the bytes matched. Amended FR-002 also owes no ask or ruling for that. So the test never operates as the struck standard. Rewriting tests that pass now would add nothing toward 'everything works'. Condition: the amended engine-plan.md and FR-002 must say this plainly. Changing the failing test is the expected response, never a reason to chase the old bytes.

decisions.summary: FR-001c is left as it is: a port task is 'straight', and skips its per-task review, only when the Python-versus-Rust comparison shows no differences.
decisions.why: FR-001c is a trigger for a review, not a standard a port must meet. A port that differs is not refused; it gets the review, and under T180 that review may not block it for bytes. The GM explicitly approved this narrower skip rule ('yes I approve the narrower rule', 2026-11-10). Widening the skip to ports with differences would undo his narrowing, which nothing in the 2026-11-18 words asks for.

decisions.summary: A bar of a quarter of re-checks, or about 10 agent-minutes a feature, labeled as the session's own reading of 'significant', not the GM's words.

I tested the 2026-11-11 'our tooling must enforce this' clause on its purpose: it targets iteration loops drifting back to running the slowest commands (10-minute full runs on every one-line edit) over and over. Two deliberate whole-file bundles, invoked with a stated reason, are not that drift class. REASON bundling remains a legitimate deliberate tool, and nothing answers wrongly.

decisions.summary: Where redrawn.rs cannot tell which kinds a change redraws (a kind chosen at run time, emit.rs building; a line of the sheet's roll, compound.rs sheet), each compound map's drawing is compared kind by kind with its drawing at the base in a new owed/marks.rs, and a kind is owed only where its marks differ.

decisions.summary: Each token goes to its own data-kind or data-part-of, else to the enclosing element's. data-id is stripped. A changed <defs> entry owes every kind that uses it, transitively.
decisions.why: Data-id stripped and per-kind attribution are the method the ruling measured with ('data-id stripped, each line attributed to its kind'). The transitive defs rule makes sure a glyph redrawn through a shared definition is still owed, so it enforces the occasion rule and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: A kind whose marks differ is owed on the first map where they differ, which moves the office hall's back-row kinds from the county (unchanged there) to the round trip (changed there).
decisions.why: A kind is owed once across the maps both before and after (the before row: the county's legend plus only the round-trip kinds the county does not draw). decisions.summary: The base text is the base commit's blob, else the mirror's copy, read as base_legends reads it.

decisions.summary: Where the marks cannot be compared, the whole legend is still owed: the hamlet driver (its marks are not read by kind), a drawing that is not current, a drawing the base does not hold, or a difference no kind owns. The occasion says which.
decisions.why: The ruling calls the whole-legend fallback a tool fault in general, and the fix leaves it in these cases, so I treat this as a narrowing. It is legitimate because per-kind comparison is physically impossible in each case: no attribution by kind (the hamlet driver), no current drawing, no base drawing, or a difference with no owning kind. In every one the fallback owes more checks, never fewer, so a glyph the occasion rule owes is never missed. The ruling measured only compound maps, so no defect is measured or known in these cases, and nothing a reader sees on a map is wrong. Each such occasion is named, so the fallback stays visible.

decisions.summary: New verb l7r-gate reviews discharge --root R --ruling TRIGGER UNIT... (owed/discharged.rs; make review-discharge RULING= UNITS=). decisions.why: The ruling asks for this route in its own words: 'If the push has no route that reads an arbiter accept as a glyph unit's discharge, that route is built with the fix and its test.' Binding to the marks digest implements 'If a sheet changes again before the push, any kind whose marks change is owed again under the rule.' The make target keeps make as the one entry point (FR-005).

decisions.summary: The verb cannot tell which units a ruling discharged, or whether the marks are the ones the ruling measured.
