decisions.summary: Takayama's residence study (a second attested form) and the armory not made knobs
decisions.why: Not asked; the join form drawn is attested on both Edo plans. Adding a knob would be scope the GM did not ask for.

decisions.summary: Ubame's household door and the hall's back door moved onto the study's back wall; household way traced clear on every sheet; county unchanged
decisions.why: The defect itself (the household entering through the clerks' room), fixed and traced on each sheet.

decisions.summary: Ochiba's visitors' way from the genkan room through the day office and clerks' room kept, a labeled GUESS
decisions.why: T375's defect, as the plan's goal states it, is the household's way, and that way is traced clear on Ochiba. O1 is the visitors' way through public office rooms; the bundle names no wrong outcome against it, and it is labeled a GUESS.

decisions.summary: The Rust tools build as one cargo workspace (root rust/Cargo.toml naming phases and guard); rust_checks.py runs each member and skips the workspace's own manifest, which builds nothing.
decisions.why: Build layout for the port the GM asked for ('making this a Rust codebase'); the checks still cover every crate (FR-004) through make (FR-005). rust_checks.py staying Python for now is allowed by FR-003 and is itself in FR-001's census, so nothing is carved out.

decisions.summary: serde_json is the one crate added.
decisions.why: A dependency choice inside the port; it narrows nothing the request or spec asks for.

decisions.summary: The guard protocol and its merge of verdicts carried from D1, D2 and contracts/guard-protocol.md.
decisions.why: Implements FR-007 (one process per tool call) and FR-002 (same verdicts); no case of the hooks is excluded.

decisions.summary: The shared state is kept and the facts are asked once.
decisions.why: Carries the measured design fixes over as FR-006 requires; no behavior the GM asked to change is preserved by it.

decisions.summary: The wrapper keeps the last good binary.
decisions.why: A build-failure fallback to an earlier Rust binary, not a return to Python; it does not run a piece twice (FR-003) and does not exempt any piece from the port.

decisions.summary: The settings switch lands with an empty guard list, its own cost recorded as phase 1's floor.
decisions.why: FR-003 keeps the Python guards the ones that run until each replacement passes, so landing the switch with no guards moved is the ordering the spec requires; recording its cost serves FR-010 and SC-001.

decisions.summary: Landed via make land-tooling with no work budget; done is both crates' tests, lint, format, cover and dead clean through make.
decisions.why: Process and exit criteria that enforce FR-004 and FR-005; nothing narrowed.

decisions.summary: T002 builds the one-process hook dispatcher answering Claude Code's protocol with an empty guard list, guards ported later
decisions.why: A first step toward FR-007 (one process per tool call) inside FR-001's hooks-first phase; ports no guard, so FR-002/FR-003 are untouched (no Python replaced, none run twice).

decisions.summary: Done when an event with no guard allows in under a millisecond of its own work and every merge case passes; --self-check answers; coverage full
decisions.why: Acceptance targets that serve SC-001/FR-007 and FR-004's coverage floor; the millisecond is a target the plan sets for the empty dispatcher, not a measured figure, and drops nothing the request or spec asks.

decisions.summary: Every merge case in contracts/guard-protocol.md tested, each test under a tenth of a second
decisions.why: Restates FR-008 and the protocol contract; enforcement of what was asked.

decisions.summary: Runs after T001, lands via make land-tooling with no work budget; red exit records the failure, sets the task down, asks the arbiter
decisions.why: Sequencing and process; the GM's request (make this a Rust codebase) is unaffected, and FR-005 keeps make as the entry point.

decisions.summary: Build the shared state every guard reads (guard log, escapes, session clone and name, GM messages) as one library that reads each fact once and writes it in today's formats.
decisions.why: Serves the request's purpose (Python hooks too inefficient, port to Rust) and FR-007 (guards as one process); 'written as today' is FR-002's same-outputs rule. Nothing the request or spec asks is dropped. Note: the block's gloss of FR-006 as 'asked once, the count pinned' is a paraphrase - FR-006 names the import graph, semantic ids and the fixture; read-once shared state is in the same spirit, not a narrowing.

decisions.summary: Green exit: a guard-log line written by Rust is read back by make guard-log exactly as the shell's is, and each read is counted once per process in a test.
decisions.why: Enforces FR-002 (same outputs) and the read-once design; verification of what was asked, not new scope.

decisions.summary: Red exit: record what failed, set the task down, route a process stop to make arbiter-ask.
decisions.why: Process routing; neither narrows nor extends the request.

decisions.summary: Runs after T002; lands via make land-tooling with no work budget; no researched value or constant moves.
decisions.why: Ordering and landing mechanics inside the hooks phase (FR-001's phase order); no requirement is relaxed.

decisions.summary: Done = the library's tests green and its reads counted.
decisions.why: Does not exempt the library from FR-004 (coverage floor) or FR-008 (test time), which still bind every replacement; the checklist omits restating them rather than carving them out.

decisions.summary: With no good binary ever built, the wrapper lets the call through with a notice and a guard-log line
decisions.why: This is plan D7's own outcome, not new in this block. It is held against FR-002, which asks for the same verdicts on every case the tests and suites hold. Having no binary at all is not one of those cases. The case that matches it today is a guard whose Python cannot start, and m:python-dead-fails-open measures that this already fails open (repo-safety exits 0 on a force push to main, make-only prints nothing, gate exits 127). So no verdict gets weaker than today's. Making it fail closed would be new behavior the GM did not ask for. The earlier BLOCKED version justified this from FR-005's make-only clause. The block now cites the requirement that actually governs verdicts.

decisions.summary: A failed build (does not compile, or compiles and fails l7r-guard --self-check) runs the last good binary; a stale build is rebuilt
decisions.why: This repeats D7 word for word, and the self-check is D7's own definition of a good build. Today a broken Python guard crashes and fails open, so keeping the previous guards running gives a verdict no weaker than today's. The request asks for a port and nothing here cuts what it covers.

decisions.summary: T004 replaces no guard; T005 adds the wrapper to the settings with an empty guard list; each guard task moves one decider in and removes that guard's shell script and settings entry in the same landing
decisions.why: This is how the plan carries out FR-003: the Python stays the one that runs until its replacement passes, and no piece runs in both. Separate processes for the guards still being moved are a temporary state. FR-007's one process is where the work ends up, and this order does not give it up.

decisions.summary: FR-005's clause that the make-only guard must cover the replacements' binaries is left to T028, not this task
decisions.why: This assigns the requirement to another task and narrows nothing. The clause is about the make-only guard's coverage, not about the wrapper. FR-005 still applies to the feature in full, and the block names the task that carries it.

decisions.summary: Lands through make land-tooling with no work budget and nothing rolled; no researched value or constant moves
decisions.why: This is process and tooling scope only. Nothing the GM asked for is changed.

decisions.summary: Every session's settings call the one dispatcher once per event, beside the Python guards it does not yet hold.
decisions.why: FR-001 ports the hooks first and FR-003 requires each unported guard's Python to stay the one that runs while no guard runs twice; FR-007's single process is the end state reached as pieces move in. A coexistence period is what FR-003 itself describes, not a carve-out from the GM's request to make this a Rust codebase.

decisions.summary: After T004; landed alone with make land-tooling.
decisions.why: Sequencing and landing route only; the spec leaves both open and neither narrows what is ported.

decisions.summary: Green: settings call it for every event, make hooks-test green, its floor timed. Red: failure recorded, task set down, process stop to make arbiter-ask.
decisions.why: The green exit enforces FR-002/FR-003 (hooks-test) and FR-010 (timed); the red exit stops rather than relaxing any requirement.

decisions.summary: No work budget, nothing rolled, for a tooling landing.
decisions.why: Process bookkeeping; it changes nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: Re-run m:hooks-bash's command with the dispatcher in place and record the floor.
decisions.why: Serves FR-010 and SC-001's measurement against m:hooks-bash; it does not claim SC-001 met or move its target.

decisions.id: T005-6 no constant or room question
decisions.summary: No researched value moves; no constant moved; not a room question.
decisions.why: Statements that the task touches only Claude Code tool-call guards, consistent with FR-009's scope and the request.

decisions.summary: Guard by guard with shell and settings entry removed in the registering commit (D3/FR-003); suite as verdict replay with its inline Python replaced in the same task (D4); order by measured cost first (R2); the two XIV fixes on make-only-hooks and guard-file-hooks (FR-002's exception).
decisions.why: Each is settled by the accepted spec (D3, D4, FR-002's named exception, FR-003) and none is T006's own: the XIV fixes belong to two other guards' tasks, so T006 changes no expected verdict. Putting pair-hooks first agrees with m:hooks-bash, which names it the slowest guard.

decisions.summary: The Rust decider keeps consulting the eight phase-3 Python tools (checkpoint.py, plan_gate.py, review_prereq.py, review_owed.py, gate-stamp.py, make engine-key, hm_arbiter.py, hm_dropped.py) by path on its two rare branches and at Stop, until each tool's own port answers in-process.
decisions.why: FR-001 fixes the phase order (hooks first, tooling in phase 3) and FR-003 requires a piece's Python to stay the one that runs until its replacement passes, so a hook ported in phase 1 has to call the tooling that is still Python. FR-007 asks for one guard process per tool call, not one per guard. It does not forbid the guard calling external tools, and the plain Bash path that SC-001/m:hooks-bash measures reaches none of them. This is temporary sequencing the spec requires, not a carve-out.

decisions.summary: The engine key (a find over l7r/ and pool/, plus make engine-key when the cache is stale) is computed only on the two branches that read it, not on every call.
decisions.why: Removing work that changes no verdict serves the request's purpose (the GM: the Python code is too inefficient), and FR-002's suite replay gates it. Two notes that are not rulings: (1) the citation is stretched, because FR-006 names three specific fixes and the plan's paraphrase 'a fact computed once, and only where it is used' is broader than the text; (2) today every call has a side effect, refreshing the cached key, and the claim that 'no other branch reads it' is shown only by the suite. If anything outside pair-hooks reads that cache and relies on the per-call refresh, FR-002's 'outputs' would cover it. Whether anything does was not measured in this bundle.

decisions.summary: The guard's inline Python state handling (pairing state, review rounds, dispatch record, bypass log, read_field) becomes Rust over the same files and formats.
decisions.why: This is the port FR-001 asks for, and keeping the same files and formats is what FR-002's same-outputs rule requires.

decisions.summary: The suite's "$HOOK" pretool|stop runs l7r-guard --only pair-hooks PreToolUse|Stop through a shared shim tests/hooks/guard-shim.sh, with the suite's cases unchanged.
decisions.why: This is D4 as written: the suite points at l7r-guard --only <guard> and its cases are unchanged. The shim only maps the suite's existing argument form onto the binary's.

decisions.summary: Green: the suite passes against the Rust guard, plus rust-test, cover and hooks-test. Red: record the failure and stop to make arbiter-ask. Landed by make land-tooling with no work budget.
decisions.why: The exits restate FR-002/FR-003/FR-004's gates, and the landing route is process that narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: hm_make.py's targets, combine and classify-through-bare-pytest move to rust/guard/src/shared/make.rs with gate-hooks, patterns verbatim; the rest of hm_make.py moves with make-only-hooks (T028) and guard-file-hooks (T029).
decisions.why: Partitions a shared library across the guards that read it; every part is still ported (FR-001, the request's 'all be ported to Rust'), verbatim patterns keep FR-002's same verdicts, and the suite replay (D4) checks the result. Nothing is left in Python that the request or spec would have ported.

decisions.summary: The decider reads tool_input.command as JSON instead of the shell's greedy sed, so a ' -k ' in the description field no longer arms the subset flag; a suite case is added, the fix named in the commit and the phase's record.
decisions.why: Applies the one exception the accepted FR-002 already states - a guard refusing correct work (a later make done refused on a falsely armed subset flag) is fixed in its port under constitution XIV - with that exception's conditions met: the case lands in the same commit and the change is named in the commit and the phase's record. It narrows nothing the GM asked for; the request is to make the codebase Rust, not to preserve a misparse.

decisions.summary: gate-hooks.sh's status mode is ported: l7r-guard --only gate-hooks status prints the same subset_pending= line, reached through the shim's status mode.
decisions.why: Preserves an existing output as FR-002 requires (same verdicts and outputs); it reverses the dropping the earlier preflight ruled NOT LEGITIMATE.

decisions.summary: After T005, independent of the other guards; green exit is the suite against l7r-guard --only gate-hooks plus rust-test, cover and hooks-test; the shell and its settings entry go in the commit that registers the decider.
decisions.why: Restates D3 (guard by guard, never both, FR-003) and D4 (the suite is the replay), and FR-004's coverage floor; no new scope.

decisions.summary: The sanitized command and the last full gate are read in-process; gatecost.py (asked only on a streak's first expensive measurement, for its reminder's median) stays the measure tool's, asked by path, until phase 3 ports it.
decisions.why: FR-001 orders the port in four phases and FR-003 keeps a piece's Python the one that runs until its replacement passes; gatecost.py belongs to a later phase, so calling it where the shell did is what those require, not a carve-out from them. It is not a guard, so FR-007's one process per tool call is not touched. Nothing the guard decides is left out of the port.

decisions.summary: The shell's greedy read (from the payload's last "command" key to its last quote) is kept for the git commit reset only, reproduced over the input in its own key order.
decisions.why: FR-002 requires the same verdicts as the shell on every suite case, and its only exception (XIV) is for a guard that refuses correct work. A later field naming git commit RESETS the streak, which makes the guard more permissive, so it refuses nothing correct, and the exception does not reach it. Keeping the shell's behavior is FR-002 applied as written. Reproducing the span over the re-serialized input rather than the raw bytes is a design choice; FR-002 judges it on the suite's cases, which the exits require to pass.

decisions.summary: status is ported, printing the same measurements_since_reset=N budget=B line.
decisions.why: FR-002: same outputs as the piece replaced.

decisions.summary: The shell guard and its settings entry are removed in the commit that registers the Rust decider, after test-measure-hooks.sh passes against l7r-guard --only measure-hooks.
decisions.why: Plan D3/D4 and FR-003 (never both), stated as accepted.

decisions.summary: hm_shape.py's wait/sleep/watch/self-matching/ceiling/periodic-report functions move to rust/guard/src/shared/wait.rs with each pattern verbatim; the rest of hm_shape.py (executing_backticks) moves with the guard that reads it
decisions.why: FR-001 replaces every tracked Python file and D3 moves guards one by one; porting the library the guard reads, patterns verbatim, is how FR-002's same-verdicts requirement is met. Nothing is left in Python or dropped - the remainder is assigned to its own guard's port.

decisions.summary: the periodic-report refusal's cron minute stays the local minute, read via `date +%M` only on the backgrounded-periodic-report branch
decisions.why: Keeps the Python's verdict and output (time.localtime().tm_min) exactly, which is what FR-002 requires; the earlier UTC alternative was the deviation and is already rejected. A child process on one rare branch is a mechanism choice, not a second guard process (FR-007 is about one process per tool call for the guards), and it changes nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: self_matching compiles the command's pgrep -f pattern with fancy-regex instead of Python re, skips a pattern it cannot compile as the Python skipped one re could not, and rests dialect-divergence detection on the suite replay
decisions.why: FR-002 scopes equivalence to every case the tests and suites hold, and D4 makes the suite the replay; the decision meets that bound, preserves the skip-on-uncompilable behavior, and states plainly that divergence outside the suite is not covered - which is the spec's own bound, not a carve-out from it. A Rust port cannot use Python's re, so a different engine is inherent to the request.

decisions.summary: The verdict library scripts/hooks/lib/hm_tree.py (judge, explain, log context) is ported whole, each pattern verbatim, to rust/guard/src/shared/tree.rs, shared with gm-tree-hooks, which moves to it in its own task.
decisions.why: FR-001 replaces every Python file and FR-002 asks for the same verdicts; porting the library the verdict comes from, verbatim, is how the guard is ported. Done-measured deletes only main-tree-hooks.sh and its settings entry, so hm_tree.py stays for gm-tree-hooks until that guard's own replacement passes (FR-003, D3).

decisions.summary: The session's clone comes from T003's session facts through the same resolver ported (claim map, last /rename, sessions json), not from spawning clone-sync-hooks.sh resolve.
decisions.why: The same resolution with the same inputs, run in the one guard process FR-007 requires; FR-002's suite replay (D4) checks the verdicts.

decisions.summary: The mirror root comes from walking up to the nearest .git (T006's find_root) and cutting at /.clones/, not from git rev-parse --show-toplevel.
decisions.why: A mechanism change stated to give the same answer, which the suite replay must confirm before the switch (FR-002, D4). It narrows nothing that was asked.

decisions.summary: The refusal and the rewrite's context name rust/guard/src/guards/main_tree_hooks.rs instead of scripts/hooks/main-tree-hooks.sh, which this task deletes; no verdict changes.
decisions.why: This is an exception to FR-002's 'same outputs', and the only exception FR-002 names is the XIV fix, so it is judged as a carve-out. Applied literally, the rule would make the guard send a refused session to a file this same commit deletes. That defeats what the message is for, which is telling the reader where the rule lives. It does not reach what FR-002 is for, proving the port changes no decision, because only the self-referencing path changes and every verdict and all other text stay as they are. The precedent is T006. If a suite case asserts the path, its expected text changes in the same commit and the commit must name that change.

decisions.summary: The hook half of scripts/measure/event_log.py (line, verdict reading, categories, log path, append) moves into the Rust decider with patterns, fields and order verbatim; the from-transcript command stays Python until phase 3 ports the measure tools.
decisions.why: The request is to make the codebase Rust; FR-001 orders the port in phases with the hooks first. The code that runs on every hook event is the hook's, and porting it with the guard is the hooks phase doing its job. The part that is a command, not a hook, goes in the later measure-tools phase, which FR-001's phase order already provides; nothing is excluded from the port. Keeping the line's fields and order the same is what FR-002 requires so that feature-report reads it unchanged.

decisions.summary: On an Edit, the reversal test (hm_arbiter.reversal) runs in-process in Rust; recording the trip is handed to hm_arbiter.py by path, and only when a reversal is found, until the arbiter is ported.
decisions.why: The arbiter is its own piece in FR-001's phase order, and this block does not port it. Calling it by path, and only on the rare reversal, keeps Python off the common path, which is the hook start-up cost the GM's request was about, and it lasts only until the arbiter's own port, so no Python is kept for good. FR-003 is per piece: the guard's verdict comes from Rust alone, so no piece runs both. The block follows T006 (a).

decisions.summary: The log line's ev is taken from the payload's hook_event_name, as the Python did; l7r-guard --only with no event name reads it from the payload, so the suite's "$HOOK" replays unchanged.
decisions.why: This keeps the Python's behavior (FR-002) and lets the guard's existing suite replay against the Rust guard without edits (D4). It is an interface detail that serves the spec and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: The edit digest stays SHA-1's first 12 hex digits, written as a small SHA-1 in shared beside T006's SHA-256 rather than taken from a crate.
decisions.why: Keeping the digest format is FR-002 (same outputs). Writing the hash in shared rather than using a crate is a design choice, not a fidelity question, and it narrows nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: The tools the guard asks (git, sync-with-main.sh, own-make.sh, gate_lock.py, clone_local_settings.py, solo.py, usage_log.py, layout_carry.sh) stay theirs and are asked by path until their own ports.
decisions.why: The request ports all the Python and the spec phases it (FR-001); FR-003 requires the Python to remain the one that runs until its replacement passes. Each tool is named as ending at its own port, so this is order, not an exclusion.

decisions.summary: The session facts the guard's inline Python read (input fields, canonical clone, whether another claimant is live) are read in-process from T003's facts and /proc; the notice's make targets use shared::make::targets.
decisions.why: This is the port itself, what the request asks for; the block binds it to the same answers, which is FR-002.

decisions.summary: The script stays as its resolve mode only, code unchanged and outside l7r-guard, until T051 deletes its callers; prompt and pretool leave in this task.
decisions.why: Sequencing, not a carve-out: (1) the kept code has a named remover, T051, so nothing is excluded from the port the request asks for and FR-001 phases; (2) the guard runs on one path, since resolve is not a guard mode and both guard modes and both settings entries go in the commit that registers the decider (item 9, D3), so FR-003 is met; (3) FR-002 is untouched, the resolve code being unchanged. The not-through-l7r-guard reasoning (recursion, cargo build) is mechanism and decides nothing here either way. Two points for the record: step 1 says 'its shell gone' while (c) keeps the script, and item 9 is the operative statement; and (b) ports the canonical-clone lookup while (c) keeps the shell's canonical_clone for the other guards, so two implementations are live until T051. That is not FR-003's 'both', each call taking one path, but T051 owes the deletion of the shell's version as well as of its callers.

decisions.summary: The prompt mode's lines are the decider's plain-stdout answer, byte for byte, so the suite's prompt cases pass unedited.
decisions.why: Directly FR-002: same outputs, suite expectations unedited.

decisions.summary: Every mode (stop, prompt, timer, stagger) moves to Rust; the detached wait and printed stagger become the binary's --idle-tests entry, started by setsid nohup as the shell was; the GM's disable of 2026-09-06 carries over as one constant, arming off.
decisions.why: Porting every mode is what the GM's 'making this a Rust codebase' and D3 ask, and leaves no shell behind. Keeping arming off is FR-002 (same verdicts), not a carve-out. FR-007's one process concerns the guards deciding a tool call, not a background wait started the way the shell started it.

decisions.summary: git, setsid, nohup, kill, pgrep and the run itself stay external tools asked by path; the lock is the flock tool on the lock file's descriptor.
decisions.why: These are system tools, not Python or shell in the repository, so FR-001 is untouched and nothing the GM asked for is reduced. The stated semantics (a lock owned by the open file the timer holds, as fd 9 was) keep FR-002. The choice of flock tool over a library call is design, which this mode does not grade.

decisions.summary: The small tools and the Python fragments go in-process (field, state_of, JSON, cksum with the same CRC values, ls -t, clone top); the JSON's keys and values are the same, its key order and indentation are not held.
decisions.why: FR-002 binds outputs 'on every case its tests and its suites hold'. Key order and indentation are outside that unless a case holds them, and if one does the block's own exit (every case of the suite passes, expectations unedited but the one in d-2) fails and the task is set down, so the obligation is not reduced. The request says nothing of byte layout. The premise that each reader takes it by key could not be checked from the bundle; the exit, not the premise, is what keeps this within.

decisions.summary: $HOOK stagger <name> reaches --idle-tests through the shim.
decisions.why: D4 points HOOK at the Rust guard; the shim routes the case's unchanged input to the entry of (a). No expectation moves.

decisions.summary: The case 'the shipped default IS disabled' grepped the shell's DEF_ARM=0; it reads the Rust constant instead.
decisions.why: This edits a case of the suite D4 makes the replay and FR-002 holds, so it is ruled on, not passed as within. The general rule is physically impossible here: the case greps a file the port must delete (D3, the GM's move to Rust), so it cannot pass unedited once the shell is gone. The case's purpose survives whole: it pins the GM's disable where that disable now lives, and its expected result is unchanged, so this is not FR-002's verdict-change exception and needs no XIV fix. It covers this one case; the block states every other expectation is unedited.

decisions.summary: Every mode of agent-stall-hooks is ported: prompt becomes the guard; check, watch, pending and ack become the binary's --agent-stall, with the Python scan done in-process and one read of each transcript's last line.
decisions.why: A complete port, which is what the request and FR-001 ask, with FR-002's same outputs. Read as: the scan the embedded Python did is now Rust code inside the Rust process. If it instead meant the binary still runs Python, it would contradict the request and FR-001; the block's goal and its 'script's logic gone' support the port reading, and the repository was not opened to confirm it.

decisions.summary: scripts/hooks/agent-stall-hooks.sh stays until T051 as a forwarder holding only a call to l7r-guard.sh --agent-stall, because this guard's report and engine-freeze-hooks' refusal print that path and sessions run watch by hand; its hook mode leaves the settings in this task (with item 9, the done-condition).
decisions.why: Does not narrow what was asked. The request and FR-001 replace Python with Rust; the forwarder is one line of shell and no Python runs. FR-003: the forwarder runs only Rust, so no piece runs both. D3 requires the settings entry to leave in the decider's commit, which the block does, and says nothing of deleting the file. FR-002: the printed command is an output, and keeping the path keeps it true. Removal at T051 is sequencing, not scope; T051's content is outside this bundle and was not checked. FR-005 (make the one entry point) is not cited by the block, but this is a hand-run path sessions already use, not a new one. Item 1's 'its shell gone' is looser than item 9, which states the actual condition; a wording tension in the plan, not a narrowing.

decisions.summary: watch still loops until killed; a tick count from the environment ends it for a unit test; the seams AGENT_STALE_S, AGENT_RECENT_S and AGENT_TICK_S are kept.
decisions.why: The tick count exists only so a test of an endless loop can meet FR-008; with FR-008 gone it has no purpose. watch's behavior is unchanged when it is unset, and keeping the existing seams serves FR-002 and D4.

decisions.summary: Ordering: after T005, in the plan's order, independent of the other guards.
decisions.why: D3's guard-by-guard order after the dispatcher lands; FR-001 puts the hooks first.

decisions.summary: Exits: the guard's suite green against l7r-guard --only agent-stall-hooks, make rust-test and cover green, make hooks-test green; on red, record and stop to make arbiter-ask.
decisions.why: D4's replay as the switch condition, FR-002 and FR-003, and FR-004's coverage floor. The red exit is process and changes nothing asked.

decisions.summary: Lands by make land-tooling with no work budget, nothing rolled.
decisions.why: Landing mechanics for tooling; it does not touch any requirement or the request.

decisions.summary: lib/stall_watchdog.py (the pass) is ported to stall_watchdog_hooks/pass.rs with the shell; prompt is the guard, run and once are the binary's --stall-watchdog
decisions.why: FR-001 puts scripts/hooks/ and the libraries its guards call in phase 1, and the GM asked for all the Python to be ported. This resolves round 1's BLOCKED on keeping the file in Python. Item 9's measured Done names the shell and settings entry but not the .py; that is an omission and not a decision to keep it, since (a) states the port and FR-001's phase-end census refuses a survivor.

decisions.summary: Each loop pass still starts a fresh process through the wrapper, so an update to what a stall is reaches a running loop

decisions.summary: archived is keyed on the URL after html.unescape, every entity; the decoding comes back as a 'plain' field of the attempts.py seen ask and reaches Rust in phase 3.

It is still a narrowing: (a) makes archived and the guard's library phase-1 Rust, and this leaves one step of archived in Python until phase 3, in a file that gains it for the guard alone. Taken on its own merits the presumption stands against it, since a full Rust decoder is possible and difficulty would not excuse it. It is legitimate only because it falls inside FR-001's by-path clause, the arbiter's ruling that stands where the GM was asked: attempts.py is a file with callers of its own, the branch is the one (c) already runs, and it adds no process and no branch. The purpose of phase 1, no Python on a plain Bash call or Edit, is untouched, and the deferral ends at a named phase, recorded in T052. UNSETTLED BY THE BUNDLE, FOR THE IMPLEMENTER UNDER FR-002: (c) reaches the ask only once a call is not blocked, so the block verdict in (b) runs on the undecoded URL, and the plan does not say whether the Python decoded before the block check or before the heredoc rule; likewise a failed ask leaves archived with no decoded key. If the Python decoded first or kept archived working when attempts.py failed, a suite case holding that must still pass, and the plan's exit (every suite case against the Rust guard) is what catches it. This ruling covers archived only and does not rule that order correct.

The block's exit (make hooks-test green) enforces it. 'Landing together' sits against D3's 'own commit', but D3 is a plan decision and FR-003's rule (no piece runs both) is unaffected.

decisions.summary: Unlabeled in the block: tests/test_agent_models.py stays Python for now and is rewired to read WAVE_JOBS from the Rust source.
decisions.why: FR-001 ports in phases, so a Python test outliving the hooks phase is the phasing as specified; the rewiring keeps the existing check pointed at the constant's new home and narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: One call stays by path until T048: hm_checks.drop_run, on a refused wave only, never a plain call; T048 ports hm_checks in the same phase and it then goes in-process.
decisions.why: FR-003 says an unported piece's Python remains the one that runs, and hm_checks is unported until T048, inside this phase. FR-007 forbids one process per guard; hm_checks is not a guard and this is one helper on a refusal path. The end state the GM asked for is unchanged and the block names the task that closes it.

decisions.summary: The Rust guards' one settings entry has its limit raised from 60 s to 600 s because a wave's units now run inside that entry.
decisions.why: No request clause or requirement sets a hook limit, and this one follows from FR-007's single process; a limit costs nothing unless a guard hangs, so SC-001 and SC-002 are untouched, and it narrows nothing. Figures: 463 ms matches m:wave-unit-hooks unit_ms 462.7; 600 s and 60 s give about 1,300 and 130 units as its quantity states; the 60 s carries a dated one-shot label; 600 s is a named knob. The MANIFEST forbids reading the repository, so m:wave-unit-hooks was not re-run; the entry as bundled shows no varies band or load.

decisions.summary: A run with no tool_use_id hashes its input as the guard's JSON writes it, where the Python's sorted-key form differed.
decisions.why: An acknowledged output difference, but FR-002 binds 'every case its tests and its suites hold', so it reaches this only if a case holds the value. Premise: the label is consumed only by the run that wrote it, no case asserts its value, and no Python side recomputes it from the input (hm_checks.drop_run in decision b is the one place that could). This could not be read from the bundle; the block's exit, every case of test-workflow-hooks.sh passing against the Rust guard, is what proves it, and a case holding the value sends the task to its red exit.

decisions.summary: The guard moves whole and in-process: its inline Python, the block pattern verbatim, both containment tests against the file on disk, the refusals' words; the reason's rule comes from shared::escape.
decisions.why: The GM asked for the Python to go to Rust (request, third quote; FR-001). Moving everything unchanged is what FR-002's same verdicts and outputs requires, in-process is FR-007, and nothing the guard does is left behind.

decisions.summary: The escape is read from the written text as the shell's was: the token anywhere in new_string plus content takes the escape branch before the file is read, and a reason short of the floor refuses there whether or not the file holds a block.
decisions.why: It keeps the existing verdict rather than changing it, which FR-002 requires; no XIV fix is claimed and no case is excepted. The claim that the shell behaves this way is the plan's reading and is not checkable from the bundle; the exit in item 6 (every suite case against the Rust guard) tests it.

decisions.summary: scripts/hooks/source-block-hooks.sh and its settings entry are gone in the commit that registers the Rust decider, after the suite passes against l7r-guard --only source-block-hooks.
decisions.why: This is D3 and D4 as written, and FR-002 (passes before deletion) and FR-003 (never both). Deleting the shell file along with its entry carries FR-001: the file holds the inline Python being replaced.

decisions.summary: Order and exits: after T005 and independent of the other guards; green is the guard's suite, make rust-test, cover and make hooks-test; red records the failure, sets the task down and stops to make arbiter-ask; landed with make land-tooling with no work budget.
decisions.why: The order follows D3's guard-by-guard landing. The exits test FR-002 and FR-004 and drop no case or requirement. The red path sets the task down instead of weakening a check, and the landing route changes nothing the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: The guard and lib/hm_shell.py both move in-process (word walk, four rules in order, rewrite and its conditions, refusal words); hm_shell.py is removed with the shell.
decisions.why: The GM asked for all the Python to be ported; FR-001 and FR-002 carry that, and the block keeps the rule order, the rewrite conditions and the refusal words. 'hm_shell.py's only caller is the guard' names no search command and could not be grepped from a bundle-only review; the ruling takes it as stated. It creates no narrowing: if another caller exists, the deletion fails rather than the scope shrinking.

decisions.summary: The suite's first line, which ran hm_shell.py --selftest, is removed and the selftest's assertions move into the guard's Rust unit tests; the corpus replay still drives the hook.
decisions.why: FR-002 and D4 require every case to hold before the Python is deleted. The assertions are moved, not dropped, and D4 already places unit tests written from the cases beside the decider. Only the line invoking a deleted Python file goes.

decisions.summary: The parse stays bash -O extglob -n, a child of the one guard process, with no Rust reimplementation of bash's grammar.
decisions.why: The request and FR-001 concern Python; bash is not Python and FR-009 shows the port's scope is bounded to it. FR-007 says one process, not one per guard: a parser child of that process is not a guard's process. Asking bash keeps the verdicts FR-002 requires, where a second parser would risk them. Cost is keyed at m:shell-check-parse.

decisions.summary: executing_backticks joins shared::shape in Rust; the Python copy in hm_shape.py stays for its other callers until T051.
decisions.why: FR-003 is per piece: this guard runs only the Rust copy, and each remaining caller runs only the Python one until its own port, as FR-003's first clause requires. No piece runs both. T051 is not in the bundle, so the deferral's placement was not checked; the Python's eventual removal is held by FR-001 regardless.

decisions.summary: This guard runs last in guards(), pinned by lib.rs's order test, with later ports inserted before it, so every other guard judges the command as written and the rewrite reaches only Claude Code.
decisions.why: Followed literally: last entry plus a pinned order means nothing after it can read the rewrite, so the defect ruled on in round 1 cannot occur and each other guard keeps the input it had as a shell guard, which FR-002 requires. The order test only enforces that. How the dispatcher aggregates several guards' results is T005's design and is not in this bundle.

decisions.summary: Green is the guard's suite against l7r-guard --only shell-check-hooks plus make rust-test, cover and hooks-test; the shell and its settings entry go in the commit that registers the decider; landed via make land-tooling.
decisions.why: This is D3 and D4 as written, with FR-004's coverage floor. The landing route and the absence of a work budget decide nothing the request or spec constrains.

decisions.summary: The guard and its decision (report, plan, held_ranges, outside_heredocs, the corrections, the three verdicts, every message) move in-process to Rust; write_targets is shared::tree::walk, the port of the walk it asked.
decisions.why: This is the port itself: the GM's 'making this a Rust codebase', FR-001 (hooks first), FR-007 (one process for a tool call) and D3 (guard by guard). Nothing asked for is left out; every message moves.

decisions.summary: lib/hm_house.py stays until its other callers are ported or T051; the guard no longer imports it.
decisions.why: Sequencing, not a carve-out. FR-003's 'no piece runs both' binds the piece, and the house-style guard runs Rust only from its switch. plan_gate.py, apply_edits.py, claims_reply.py, hm_arbiter.py, check-house-style-delta.py and hookbench.py are other pieces, and until each is replaced FR-003 itself requires that its Python remain the one that runs. FR-001 still takes the file, with T051 as the named end.

decisions.summary: The word table becomes a data file, rust/guard/src/guards/house_style_words.tsv, generated from hm_house.py's table; test_house_style_delta.py's reading holds the two equal; the guard's and check-house-style-delta.py's exempt names gain the data file.
decisions.why: A data file is not Python, so FR-001 is met. The equality test only enforces FR-002's sameness while two copies exist, which is enforcement of what was asked. The exemption is an exception in form but narrows nothing: the table is out of the corrector's reach today where it lives, the port moves it, and the exemption moves with it, so the table's treatment is unchanged. The path is new, so no suite case's verdict can move. A table of wrong spellings run through the corrector would stop being that table.

decisions.summary: The crash warning goes: the shell told the session when its Python decision could not run; a compiled decision has no import to fail, and a guard that does not run is the wrapper's own notice (T004).
decisions.why: FR-002 requires the same verdicts AND outputs, its named exceptions do not cover this, and the warning is an output, so this is a narrowing and is presumed wrong. It is legitimate on the impossibility leg: the warning reports that a Python decision failed to run, the port leaves no Python decision to fail, and emitting it would state something false. Its purpose, the session being told its guard did not decide, passes to the wrapper's notice (T004) rather than being dropped. The ruling rests on two premises this bundle cannot confirm, the repository being closed to this review. First, the import-stub case asserts the act, as (e) says, and not the warning line; D4 is the backstop, since a case expecting that line fails against l7r-guard --only house-style-hooks and stops the switch, and editing such a case would have to be named as FR-002's exceptions are. Second, 'no import to fail' does not by its own words reach the data file (c) creates: if the table is read at runtime, a missing or malformed file is the failure this warning existed for, and it must then reach the session through T004's notice or be compiled in. Silence on that failure is outside this ruling.

decisions.summary: The suite's import-stub case keeps its assertion that the guard still acts on a command with hm_house.py broken, now by driving the link with the module broken in a copy of the tree; its verdict does not change.
decisions.why: D4 points the suite at the Rust guard, and this adapts how the case reaches it. The assertion and expected verdict are kept, so FR-002's bookkeeping for a changed verdict is not engaged. What the case proves after the port is a question of test value, not fidelity.

decisions.summary: This guard runs before shell-check (T035 decision (d)), so shell-check judges the corrected text, whose words differ only in spelling or dash; shell-check's four rules read neither.
decisions.why: The ordering was settled by T035 (d) and is only cited here; one process (FR-007) requires some order. The block states why FR-002's sameness holds under it and claims no exception, and both guards' suites must stay green at the exit.

decisions.summary: The guard and its library both move in-process (arming, once-per rules, question and offer patterns, transcript reading, kept-question naming, every message); lib/hm_gm_question.py is removed with the shell.
decisions.why: The request is to port the Python, all of it; FR-001 and D3 carry this, and moving every message serves FR-002. The claim that the guard is the library's only caller names no search command and could not be checked from the bundle; taken as stated, it is not a narrowing of the request.

decisions.summary: scripts/reviews/ledger_lint.py stays Python and is called by path from the Rust guard, for the row count when a review arms and for 'every finding disposed' at a turn's end with a review armed.
decisions.why: This narrows FR-007 (one process for a tool call), which the block does not cite: an Agent dispatch is a tool call and it would start a Python child. The rarity argument is not the ground of this ruling. The ground is that the request's 'all be ported' is reduced in timing only: ledger_lint.py is a tracked Python file, so FR-001 and SC-005's censuses require it gone before the feature closes, and T052's record is where the block tracks it; the stay cannot be permanent. Porting it inside T044 is not open either: it has callers of its own, so a Rust copy in the guard beside the Python tool would be one piece run twice, against FR-003 and D3's one-at-a-time rule. Purpose test: the GM's complaint is Python's cost, and a transitional spawn on these branches does not gut it. Both branches, Agent dispatch and Stop, were weighed separately and stand on the same ground. 'Never a plain Bash call or Edit' is a claim about which events reach these branches, not measured in the bundle and taken as stated; the ruling does not rest on it. The ruling covers the transitional stay only: a call to Python surviving ledger_lint's own port would not be covered.

decisions.summary: state, arm and disarm become a command line of the binary, --escalation, like the other guards' non-hook modes; the seams still refuse a path outside a fixture.
decisions.why: How the ported subcommands are reached is left open by the spec. FR-005 is the only requirement it touches and the block does not contradict it; keeping the seam's refusal preserves behavior under FR-002.

decisions.summary: clone_of walks up for .git in-process, the answer git rev-parse --show-toplevel gives, so no process starts on an Agent call or a Stop.
decisions.why: An implementation choice inside the port, serving FR-007 and held to FR-002 by the suite replay (D4).

decisions.summary: The proof of equal verdicts is the guard's suite run against l7r-guard --only escalation-hooks, with unit tests written from its cases (item 2's 'every suite case', items 6 and 9).
decisions.why: D4 settles the suite as the replay for a guard. FR-002's text is wider, 'every case its tests and its suites hold', and the block paraphrases it as suite cases only. If lib/hm_gm_question.py has tests of its own, FR-002 reaches them before the deletion; the bundle does not show whether it does, so no narrowing is found on the evidence available.

decisions.summary: The guard and its library hm_review_round.py both move in-process and are removed; the one Python test importing the library moves, plan_rounds and the third-round rule to the guard's unit tests, the real arbiter round trip to a new suite case.
decisions.why: FR-001 applied to this guard's own files, and D3's guard-by-guard move. Nothing the guard decides is left behind ('every refusal', 'both caps'). The test move carries the test's cases rather than dropping them (FR-002), and the slow round trip goes to the suite because FR-008 holds unit tests under a tenth of a second.

decisions.summary: Three record tools (hm_arbiter.py, plan_gate.active_task, stale_terms.py) stay Python and are called by path, each only on a spec-fidelity dispatch, none on a plain Bash call or Edit.
decisions.why: Read as sequencing, not an exemption: FR-001 replaces every Python file in four phases and SC-005 requires the census empty at close, so these three are not excused from the port, only from this guard's piece. This rests on the block's own references: hm_arbiter.py is named T051's, and T052's record lists all three; each has callers of its own, so it is not this guard's library. A reading in which any of the three stays Python past the feature's close would narrow FR-001 and would not be covered by this ruling. FR-003 holds (each runs as Python only, never both). FR-007 is about one process per tool call for the guards; these are record tools, not guards, and SC-001's Bash-call figure is untouched because none runs on a Bash call.

decisions.summary: The diff is difflib.unified_diff ported exactly in shared::difflib (SequenceMatcher with default autojunk, opcode grouping, headers), pinned byte for byte by difflib_cases.json, cases generated from CPython's difflib.
decisions.why: Round 1's objection was that diff -u's edits differ from difflib's, breaking FR-002's same outputs. The port removes that. Default autojunk is not a choice but the literal behavior: CPython's unified_diff builds SequenceMatcher(None, a, b) with no autojunk argument, so the default is what the Python guard runs. The pin only fails when the requested sameness is absent, so it enforces FR-002 and is not added scope. The ruling rests on the block's exactness claim and D4's suite replay; the bundle does not show the Rust.

decisions.summary: state and the suite's verdict-of become a command line of the binary, --review-round; verdict-of replaces the suite's import of the deleted module, its case and verdict unchanged.
decisions.why: A consequence of removing the module under FR-001: the suite needs another route to the same reading, and the block keeps the case and verdict unchanged, so FR-002 and D4's replay stand. It changes the fixture's plumbing, not what any case asserts, and adds no behavior beyond what the deleted module offered.

decisions.summary: Order (after T005, independent of the other guards), exits (suite green against l7r-guard --only review-round-hooks, rust-test, cover, hooks-test), and done (shell and settings entry gone in the commit registering the decider); landed by make land-tooling with no work budget.
decisions.why: D3 and D4 restated for this guard: the settings entry leaves in the same commit that adds the decider, after the suite passes, so FR-003's never-both holds. Cover green serves FR-004. No researched value moves.

decisions.summary: The guard and its deciding move (classify, doubled_var, the targeted-pytest and entry-point rewrites, every refusal's words) ported in-process.
decisions.why: The port FR-001 and the request ask for, held to FR-002's same verdicts and words. The whole section was judged: earlier.md says every block is new, so the bundle carries no earlier text and no prior verdict to diff against.

decisions.summary: lib/hm_make.py stays for hookmatch.py, guard-file-hooks.sh and test_guard_corpus.py until T051.
decisions.why: FR-003 forbids one piece running both. This guard runs only Rust once switched; the library stays for other pieces not yet ported, each of which runs one implementation (D3, guard by guard).

decisions.summary: test_guard_firing_log.py's named list drops this guard; make_only_hooks/tests.rs an_escape_is_recorded_with_its_reason takes the guarantee in the same commit.
decisions.why: Classed narrowing because an existing check loses a named entry, and FR-002 holds the piece to every case its tests hold. Ruled on the bundle alone; T034's ruling is not in it and was not relied on. Physically impossible to keep: the block states the test scans shell permit sites, and D3 removes this guard's shell in that commit, so the entry would have nothing to scan. The purpose survives: the named test goes red if the escaped branch writes no firing record, and it lands in the same commit, so the guarantee is never absent. Premise, stated by the block and not measurable from the bundle: the Python test only scans shell permit sites, and there is one escaped branch for the Rust test to cover.

decisions.summary: XIV fix: a grep whose pattern names pytest is not a pytest run; shared::make::pytest_view blanks a searcher's quoted -c pattern and drops an escaped pipe; gate's bare_pytest reads the same view.
decisions.why: FR-002 names this exception and its conditions, and the block meets each: a guard refusing correct work fixed in its port, the expected verdict changed in the same commit, named in the commit and in phase 1's record. It narrows nothing asked. A pipe or command outside the quoted pattern is untouched, so a real pytest run is still seen. Any gate case whose verdict moves through the shared view falls under the same naming duty.

decisions.summary: A direct Bash run of a replacement's binary (l7r-guard, hamlet, by any path) refused with the make target that runs it, new verdict bare-binary beside bare-cargo, new suite cases.
decisions.why: FR-005's clause, carried as the requirement says. A new verdict on new cases moves no existing case under FR-002. Naming the two binaries is this task's reach; FR-005 and SC-005 still hold any later replacement's binary to the same cover.

decisions.summary: The wrapper scripts/hooks/l7r-guard.sh is not the binary and passes.
decisions.why: Classed narrowing because it is an except inside the FR-005 cover and it runs the binary. Legitimate because FR-005's own words set the boundary: the rule covers the replacements' binaries, as the guard covers the Python and cargo today, and a shell wrapper is none of those, so FR-002's same verdicts govern it. It is one file, reaches only the guard, and leaves every path to the binary itself refused. Premise, from FR-005's wording and not verifiable from the bundle: today's guard does not refuse a direct Bash run of a hook script under scripts/hooks/. If it does, FR-005's parity clause would require the same refusal and this ruling would not hold.

decisions.summary: ruff stays by path on a make land-tooling or arbiter-fix-done naming a .py file; T052's record lists it.
decisions.why: Classed narrowing because a Python tool stays in the ported guard of a feature asked to end Python. Legitimate for now: FR-001 replaces tracked Python files and ruff is not one, FR-002 requires this branch's output unchanged, and dropping it while tracked .py files remain would stop linting them without serving the port. The purpose is not gutted, because the branch only fires on a .py file and has nothing to do once the last one goes. Limit of this ruling: it covers the period while tracked .py files exist. Being listed in T052's record is not removal, and SC-005 still decides at close whether it may remain.

decisions.summary: Order after T005 and independent of the other guards; exits on the suite against l7r-guard --only make-only-hooks with FR-005's new cases; the shell and its settings entry gone in the commit that registers the decider; red goes to make arbiter-ask.
decisions.why: These restate D3, D4 and FR-005. Nothing is added or relaxed beyond them. No figure with a unit stands in the block except FR-008's tenth of a second, a quotation of the requirement.

decisions.summary: The guard moves whole and in-process; git is asked only for a held file or a /Makefile path.
decisions.why: FR-001, FR-002 and FR-007 ask for exactly this; every message and rule moves, none is dropped.

decisions.summary: hm_guard_permit.py stays for its grant, run by guard-edit; the guard reads the store itself; T051 owes the file.
decisions.why: Phase order under FR-001: the piece that still has a Python caller stays until its own task, named. FR-003 holds, the deciding moves once.

decisions.summary: The amended clause: the storing target is cat's one redirect or each of tee's file arguments, each a word of plain path characters and $NAME expansions.
decisions.why: FR-002's XIV exception, the logged scratch-file refusal. The clause closes what the last round found: process substitution, command substitution and backquote are out of the opener. A $NAME is not re-parsed: run 2026-11-08 under bash 5.3.9, a value holding >(...) given to tee only named literal files, one holding $(...) on a redirect was an ambiguous redirect, neither ran.

decisions.summary: The closed form admits any NAME=value of a plain value before the storing command, PATH included, and states that then no command in the call can run what was stored.
decisions.why: The sentence is false for this member of the form. Run 2026-11-08, bash 5.3.9, with a directory holding a symlink named cat to python3: both a PATH=<dir> prefix on the storing cat and a PATH=<dir> line before it, one call, quoted delimiter, nothing after the terminator, ran the body as Python (a marker file appeared); the real cat as control ran nothing. That is the form the same decision keeps refused, a body handed to an interpreter, and the verdict would change to pass, past the 'one form alone' it promises and past FR-002's exception, which reaches only correct work refused. The setup is one earlier call, and the logged case needs none of it. Fix: no assignment in the call may name PATH or a dynamic-loader variable (LD_*), and a refused case in test-make-only-hooks.sh pins it. Not reopened: the forms already refused; and the store-then-run-in-a-later-call route, which the sentence's 'in the call' leaves out.

decisions.summary: T053 changes record-edit only: check-bundle runs on an Agent call alone and checks-hooks.sh after greps its state in shell, so neither starts Python on a plain call.
decisions.why: FR-001's clause is that none of the three may start Python on a plain Bash call or plain Edit; a guard that already does not needs no change. The premise is a dated reading with its sources named. The ruling ask:449-hm-checks-route is settled and not reopened.

decisions.summary: The test of whether a call can concern the guard moves to Rust; record-edit-hooks.sh runs unchanged behind it and its reply becomes the binary's answer.
decisions.why: FR-001 puts the guard and hm_checks/hm_record in phase 3 and requires only that until then they not start Python on a plain call; a filter in front is that arrangement. The gate reads the state and writes nothing, so one implementation still writes checks-open.json. It is not two implementations of one decision under FR-003: the deciding stays in the Python alone.

decisions.summary: A Bash call that names apply-edits or runs make done by hm_checks' own pattern starts the shell guard.
decisions.why: These are the commands the guard exists for, not plain calls.

decisions.summary: While a plan review holds text, EVERY Bash call starts the shell guard and so Python, including an unrelated ls.
decisions.why: This is a real carve-out from 'never on a plain Bash call' and is ruled on its own. Applying the rule literally defeats the purpose: any command can rewrite held text, so no narrower test on the command exists, skipping Python would drop the hold's verdicts against FR-002, and the deciding cannot move to Rust before phase 3 because the settled ruling ports it in one cut. It is confined to the span of a plan review's hold, the 'rare branch' FR-001 names, and ends in phase 3.

decisions.summary: An Edit or Write starts the shell guard when its file is one subject_of_path freezes or page_dir_for re-aims.
decisions.why: Those files are what the guard acts on, so such an Edit is not a plain one.

decisions.summary: During a hold, only an Edit or Write of a specs/*/plan.md reaches the guard; any other file starts nothing.
decisions.why: Round 1's NOT LEGITIMATE item is cured. The change moves toward the request's clause: an Edit of an unrelated file during a hold is the plain case and now starts no Python.

decisions.summary: The gate treats Write as it treats Edit, though the goal and FR-001 say plain Edit.
decisions.why: record-edit's settings entry covers Edit and Write together; the same filter serves the same clause and adds no behavior.

decisions.summary: The state is found as hm_checks.state_path finds it, a .git file resolved through its gitdir and commondir.
decisions.why: Round 1's NOT LEGITIMATE fallback is gone; this is the Python's own resolution carried over, so the hold is seen in a worktree.

decisions.summary: With no repository there is no state and so no hold, as state_path returning None gives.
decisions.why: Round 1's NOT LEGITIMATE fallback is gone; the case now matches the Python it fronts.

decisions.summary: FR-007 is read as one process on a plain call; a call that concerns the guard runs the Rust binary, the shell guard and Python.
decisions.why: FR-007 is unconditional and this is less than it says, so it is ruled. FR-001's phase-3 clause keeps this guard's Python until phase 3 and bars it only on a plain call, so one process on a concerning call is impossible before that cut. It is transitional and ends with the phase-3 port.

decisions.summary: Before T050-T052, the phase's close measures it; exits by suite, rust-test, cover and hooks-test, a red exit to arbiter-ask; no work budget.
decisions.why: Sequencing and process inside the feature; nothing asked for is reduced.

decisions.summary: The four tests/hooks Python helpers ported as l7r-guard subcommands and crate tests.
decisions.why: FR-001, phase 1's tests/hooks Python.

decisions.summary: Unused libraries deleted with their last caller.
decisions.why: FR-001: nothing is left behind by the port.

decisions.summary: The close on SC-001 and phase 1's share of both censuses empty.
decisions.why: FR-001 re-runs both censuses at each phase's end; FR-010 records the timings.

decisions.summary: A hand lexer for three Python facts rather than a parser crate, held to the Python's answers by a differential.
decisions.why: How the port is built; FR-002's same outputs are what m:t050-deps-differential compares.

decisions.summary: The name index keeps the dict's first-place, last-path semantics.
decisions.why: FR-002: the same outputs as the Python replaced.

decisions.summary: Traces kept before the port stand: the directory entries, blob id and git calls are reproduced in Rust so no suite re-runs for the port alone.
decisions.why: FR-002 applied to the keys.

decisions.summary: One python3 process per fresh or stamp call for sys.version, never a hook's, gone with the last Python a suite runs at phase 3's end, listed in T052's record.
decisions.why: A Rust tool in phase 1 still starts Python, which neither census can see. It stands on three things: the key's value is sys.version, which only the interpreter can state exactly, and the key must equal the kept traces' under FR-002; it is never on a hook path, so it does not touch the cost the GM's request was about or the limit in ask:449-phase1-tools-by-path; and it has a stated exit tied to the Python it describes. The exit is what makes it legitimate, not its low cost. The closing sentence that staying would 'break nothing' earns it nothing: FR-001's phase 4 removes the Python the container installs, so past that point the spawn has no interpreter to start.

decisions.summary: bench drops feature 239's refusal of a guard with no importable decision, on the ground that every guard's decision is in this binary now; only an unknown name is refused.
decisions.why: Removing a recorded refusal changes a tool's output (FR-002, SC-004), and the only ground offered is a factual premise that FR-001 contradicts: its last sentence puts check-bundle, checks and record-edit in phase 3, with their libraries, so at T050 those three are not ported. The refusal existed so the cost of spawning stayed visible, and for those three that purpose survives. The block does not say what bench does with them: refused as unknown, measured by spawn and labeled, or something else.
